sampler_discrepancy.observation: In both runs, the --rss-samples 1 Hz VmRSS series stays flat near baseline (~170-196 MB) for the entire 120 s run, while /usr/bin/time -v's lifetime 'Maximum resident set size' for the same process is ~1.9-2.0 GB.
sampler_discrepancy.interpretation: Most consistent with a fast-appearing, fast-receding native-heap allocation spike (e.g. large glibc mmap-backed allocations made and munmap'd within a sub-second window, or per-thread malloc-arena churn across the 64 client threads) rather than a value that climbs and holds steady across the step -- exactly the kind of native-allocator behavior the P-OV1 README already flagged as invisible to tracemalloc, and it turns out to be coarse-grained-RSS-polling-invisible too. Pinning the exact allocation site would need finer-grained sampling (e.g. 100 ms VmRSS polling, or mallinfo2()/malloc_stats() snapshots) -- out of scope for this bounded diagnostic and left as a follow-up.
sampler_discrepancy.does_not_change_the_verdict: This affects only the --rss-samples time series' usefulness for localizing WHEN the spike happens; the --no-call-records ablation below is a between-run comparison of /usr/bin/time -v's peak (a full-process, allocator-visible measurement in both runs), which is unaffected by the polling gap.

verdict.reasoning: Disabling the harness's own per-call retention entirely (--no-call-records: no CallRecord list, no 76,800-entry .records.json written) changed the process's peak RSS by about 0.6% (1,991,888 KB with records vs 2,004,096 KB without -- the no-call-records run is if anything slightly HIGHER, within run-to-run noise). If the multi-GB growth were harness-side bookkeeping (the CallRecord list plus its end-of-sweep JSON serialization, as the P-OV1 tracemalloc note suspected but could not confirm past ~83 MB), removing that retention should have collapsed the peak toward the ~150-200 MB baseline seen in the low-rate/1-client steps. It did not. Both peaks are two orders of magnitude above what tracemalloc's harness-side accounting could ever explain (it only ever attributed ~83 MB), and now also above what removing that accounting removes (~0 MB of the ~2 GB). The growth is therefore attributable to something outside scripts/eval_overload.py's own Python-level bookkeeping -- most plausibly the native engine (tgms._engine, a Rust .so) or glibc allocator behavior triggered by 64 concurrently-calling threads hammering ToolRouter/ConcurrencyGate at once, not Python-level result retention by either class (grep of tgms/tools/server.py and tgms/tools/limits.py finds no accumulating list/history field on ToolRouter or ConcurrencyGate -- neither class retains past call results, so 'result retention' in the literal sense is also ruled out as the mechanism, leaving native-heap/allocator behavior under thread concurrency as the leading candidate).
verdict.not_pinned_down: This diagnostic identifies WHERE the growth is not (harness CallRecord retention, ToolRouter/ConcurrencyGate result history, the edge-postings index, the byte-budget segment cache) but does not identify the exact native allocation site -- that would need native-side profiling (e.g. Valgrind/massif, jemalloc/glibc arena instrumentation, or per-thread RSS breakdown) against tgms._engine, which is out of scope for this bounded (~10 min) measurement.
